summary: Describes a tunnel for carrying Ethernet over IPv6 with a mandatory 64-bit cookie, connecting Layer 2 attachment circuits identified by IPv6 addresses. It is based on L2TPv3 over IP and does not use the L2TPv3 control plane.

eli5.summary: A secret tunnel for network cables over IPv6. Each packet carries a long secret number so the receiver knows it belongs there.

questions: ethernet over ipv6 tunnel with cookie
what is a keyed ipv6 tunnel
why does l2tpv3 use a 64 bit cookie
subtitle: Ethernet over IPv6 tunnels with no control plane, one tunnel per IPv6 address pair and a mandatory 64-bit cookie.

tldr.problem: L2TPv3 usually multiplexes many Layer 2 circuits over one tunnel using a Session ID. With IPv6's huge address space, each circuit can instead have its own IPv6 address.
tldr.mechanism: Each tunnel has exactly one session, configured by the management plane at both ends with no L2TPv3 control plane. Every packet carries a 64-bit cookie that the receiver checks, and Ethernet frames ride directly over IPv6 with no UDP.
tldr.outcome: Tunnels are identified by IPv6 addresses, which gives better ECMP load balancing and finer control over advertising endpoints. The cookie guards against blind spoofing but is not a substitute for IPsec.

facts.label: Control plane
facts.value: None; management plane configures both ends

today: RFC 8159 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification of this keyed IPv6 tunnel encapsulation.

sections.title: Why a Keyed IPv6 Tunnel
sections.content:
L2TPv3 (RFC 3931) tunnels Layer 2 circuits across an IP network. Normally many attachment circuits share one pair of IP endpoints and the L2TPv3 Session ID tells them apart.

Over IPv6 there is a different option. IPv6 offers a vast number of unique addresses, so each Ethernet attachment circuit can be identified directly by an IPv6 address. Each tunnel then has one and only one session, and processing of the Session ID can be bypassed on receipt. This does not stop the same router from using Session IDs for other L2TPv3 tunnels.

The RFC lists two advantages over the traditional approach of terminating on a loopback address: better ECMP load balancing, since every tunnel has a unique source and destination IPv6 address pair, and finer-grained control when advertising tunnel endpoints in a routing protocol.
sections.eli5: Normally lots of cables share one big pipe and get sorted by a number. With IPv6 there are so many addresses that each cable can have its own pipe.

sections.title: Static 1:1 Mapping Without a Control Plane
sections.content:
The L2TPv3 control plane is not used. Instead the management plane creates and maintains matching configurations at both ends of each tunnel. This sets up a one-to-one mapping between the access-side Ethernet attachment circuit (a port ID, or a port ID plus VLAN IDs) and a local IPv6 address on the network side. That address also identifies the tunnel endpoint.

These local IPv6 addresses SHOULD NOT come from connected subnets facing the remote endpoints, because that would create an IPv6 Neighbor Discovery cache entry per tunnel on the next-hop router. It is RECOMMENDED to assign them from dedicated subnets used only for tunnel endpoints.

Some deployments use a single unicast or anycast IPv6 address for a service instance, such as a virtual switch, across several tunnels. Then the decapsulating device uses the local address to find the service instance and the remote address to find the tunnel.

For compatibility with existing RFC 3931 implementations, packets are still sent with a Session ID. Because Session ID processing is not enabled, there can be only a single keyed IPv6 tunnel between two IPv6 addresses.
sections.eli5: There is no phone call to set up the pipe. Someone writes the same settings on both ends ahead of time, and each end knows exactly which cable goes with which address.

sections.title: The Mandatory 64-Bit Cookie
sections.content:
The cookie is an extra tunnel endpoint context check. 64 bits is the largest cookie size permitted in RFC 3931. All packets MUST carry the 64-bit cookie, and it MUST be 64 bits long to protect against spoofing and brute-force blind insertion attacks. Values SHOULD be randomly selected.

With no control plane, the encapsulating router MUST be given the cookie by local configuration for each local and remote IPv6 endpoint. Cookies are asymmetric: the two ends can and SHOULD send different values. A cookie MUST be changeable at any time without dropping legitimate packets, so the receiver MUST be configurable to accept two cookies for one tunnel at once, the old and the new. The management plane SHOULD change cookies periodically.

Mandating a 64-bit cookie differs from the optional variable-length cookie in RFC 3931. The management plane MUST NOT configure a keyed IP tunnel unless both endpoints support the 64-bit cookie.
sections.eli5: The cookie is a long secret number written on every envelope. If the number on an envelope is wrong, the receiver throws it away. Two numbers are allowed at once while the secret is being swapped.

sections.title: The Encapsulation
sections.content:
The ingress router encapsulates the whole Ethernet frame, without the preamble and Frame Check Sequence (FCS), in L2TPv3 as in RFC 4719. The L2TPv3 packet rides directly over IPv6, with no UDP header. Retaining the FCS (RFC 4720) is OPTIONAL and, if supported, MUST be configurable and consistent at both ends. All routers MUST be able to send and receive frames without the FCS. Service-delimiting VLAN IDs (S-tag, C-tag, or both) have local significance and MUST NOT be forwarded over the tunnel.

  • IPv6 header: the traffic class may be set for per-hop behavior and QoS, and the flow label (RFC 6437) may be set for finer-grained ECMP. The next header is 0x73, meaning L2TPv3.
  • Session ID: with one-stage resolution (IPv6 address only) it SHOULD be ignored on receipt. Setting it to all ones (0xFFFFFFFF) is RECOMMENDED for easy troubleshooting. A Session ID of zero MUST NOT be used, since it is reserved for L2TP control messages. The Session ID is unidirectional.
  • Cookie: all packets for a circuit MUST match one of the cookies configured for it, and others MUST be discarded.
  • L2-Specific Sublayer: present only if VCCV or frame sequencing is required. Bit 0 is the V-bit for VCCV messages, and bit 1 is the S-bit meaning a valid sequence number is in bits 8-31.
sections.eli5: The whole Ethernet frame goes into an IPv6 envelope. On the envelope are the secret cookie and a label saying 'this holds a tunnel packet'.

sections.title: Fragmentation and OAM
sections.content:
Encapsulating Ethernet in IPv6 reduces the effective MTU for the carried traffic. The recommended fix is for the operator to raise the MTU on all links between tunnel endpoints so the IPv6 packet needs no fragmentation. Routers are RECOMMENDED to implement IPv6 Path MTU discovery (RFC 1981). They MAY implement L2TPv3 fragmentation, configured per tunnel and consistent at both ends. Enabling plain IPv6 fragmentation for keyed tunnels is NOT RECOMMENDED.

OAM matters more without a control plane, because it becomes the only way to detect failures in the tunnel overlay. Underlay failures can be found through the routing protocol and single-hop BFD, and multihop BFD MAY be enabled between endpoints. Because tunnel-layer OAM cannot see failures in Ethernet service processing or on the attachment circuit, Ethernet OAM (IEEE 802.1ag and/or Y.1731) is RECOMMENDED, using an Up MEP toward the tunnel, a Down MEP toward the local circuit, and a MIP for intermediate checks. Pseudowire VCCV MAY also be used. The management plane is RECOMMENDED to act when a circuit failure is detected, for example by dropping the remote attachment circuit.
sections.eli5: The envelope makes the package a bit bigger, so the road has to be wide enough. With no phone line between the ends, they must check on each other another way to notice a broken pipe.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packet spoofing is a particular worry for VPN tunneling: carefully built rogue packets inserted into the transit network could break VPN traffic separation and leak data into a customer VPN. Keyed IPv6 encapsulation separates traffic by using separate 128-bit IPv6 addresses for endpoints, and the mandatory 64-bit cookie is an extra check that a packet is meant for the identified tunnel.

Against blind spoofing, the cookie protects against inadvertent leaking of frames into a customer VPN, and the cookie MUST be used on all tunnels to resist brute-force blind insertion. It offers no protection against a sophisticated man-in-the-middle who can sniff and correlate captured data. It must not be regarded as a substitute for security such as IPsec on an open or untrusted network.
sections.eli5: The secret number stops people who are guessing blindly. It does not stop someone who can read the envelopes along the way, so use a stronger lock like IPsec on risky roads.

fields.name: IPv6 Header
fields.desc: Next header 0x73 (L2TPv3); traffic class and flow label may be set.

fields.name: Session ID
fields.desc: Ignored on receipt with one-stage resolution; zero is never used.

fields.name: Cookie (0:31)
fields.desc: First half of the mandatory 64-bit cookie.

fields.name: L2-Specific Sublayer (optional)
fields.desc: Only for VCCV and/or frame sequencing.
